name: Strawberry
summary: How strawberry is grown in the cool highlands of Benguet, where nearly all Philippine strawberries come from: runners set on raised beds after the typhoon months and berries picked from about December to May. Lowland farms can only grow a few plants in pots, so this guide is for upland growers.
season: Strawberry needs cool days, about 14 to 23 degrees, to form flower buds, so it is grown mainly around La Trinidad and other high places in Benguet. Open field growers plant after the heavy rains and typhoons, around October to November, and pick from about December up to April or May, the coldest and driest months. Rain spoils the berries, so open field picking lasts about six months.
material: Runners, the young daughter plants that grow on stems from a mother plant. Mother plants make runners in the warm, long days from May to August, and growers root them in small bags or beds before setting them out. Many farmers favor the variety Sweet Charlie for its sweetness, and clean, disease free planting stock is worth buying.
spacing: Raised beds about 1.5 meters wide and 16 to 20 cm high, with plants about 25 cm apart in rows along the bed.
water: Frequent light watering by hose, sprinkler or furrow so the shallow roots never dry, with good drainage so water does not stand. Water is scarce in some strawberry areas, so mulch helps a lot.
fertilizer: Organic fertilizer or well rotted manure, about 5 tons for a hectare, split between bed making and about a month after planting. Some growers add an organic foliar feed every two weeks.
care: Mulch of plastic or rice straw on the beds, regular weeding, and pinching of runners and dead leaves while the plants bear. Pests are watched closely, with yellow sticky traps, soap spray and removal of spotted leaves, and crops are rotated to cut soil diseases.
harvest: Berries are picked fully or nearly all red, in the cool morning, every two or three days, from about December to April or May in the open field. They are held by the stalk, laid in shallow trays, kept in the shade and sold within a day or two, because they bruise and spoil fast.

ways.label: Rooted runners (anak ng strawberry)

steps.title: Pick healthy runners
steps.how: Take well rooted runners only from strong, healthy mother plants, or buy clean planting stock. Throw away runners with spotted or curled leaves.

steps.title: Choose and hoe the field
steps.how: Pick a gentle, well drained upland field near water and easy to reach by road. Hoe the soil two or three times to break it up and kill weeds.

steps.title: Raise the beds and add compost
steps.how: Make raised beds about 16 to 20 cm high and about 1.5 meters wide. Work organic fertilizer or well rotted manure into the beds. About 5 tons for a hectare is split between now and later.

steps.title: Cover the beds
steps.how: Many growers cover the beds with plastic mulch or rice straw so the berries stay clean and the soil stays moist. Punch planting holes in rows along the bed.

steps.title: Set out the runners
steps.how: Plant the runners about 25 cm apart, with the crown sitting right at the soil surface, neither buried nor exposed. Water them in well.

steps.title: Water often, never soggy
steps.how: Water the beds every few days in dry weather by hose, sprinkler or furrow so the roots never dry out, but drain off any standing water.

steps.title: Replace weak plants
steps.how: Replace runners that died or stay limp after the first week.

steps.title: Weed and feed
steps.how: Pull weeds from the planting holes and paths. Every two weeks some growers spray a mild organic foliar feed such as vermi tea.

steps.title: Scout for pests and leaf spots
steps.how: Check under the leaves for aphids and spider mites, which leave fine webbing, and look for cutworms, armyworms and slugs at night. Yellow sticky traps and a mild soap spray help, and spotted leaves should be removed.

steps.title: Second dose of compost
steps.how: Give the second share of the organic fertilizer along the rows and water it in.

steps.title: Pinch runners and old leaves
steps.how: While the plants bear, pinch off new runners and dead leaves so the plant puts its strength into the berries.

steps.title: Pick ripe berries
steps.how: Pick berries that are fully or nearly all red, in the cool of the morning, every two or three days. Hold the stalk, not the berry, and lay them in shallow trays.

steps.title: Keep them cool
steps.how: Keep the trays in the shade, do not stack them high, and sell the berries within a day or two.

steps.title: Keep mother plants for runners
steps.how: When the season ends, keep the healthiest plants as mother plants on a clean bed. Let them make runners from May to August for the next planting.

parts.title: Choose the mother plants
parts.how: Keep only vigorous, disease free plants about a year old, of the variety you want, as mothers. Leave behind plants with spotted, curled or mottled leaves.

parts.title: Set them on a clean bed
parts.how: Plant the mothers on a raised bed about 16 to 20 cm high, about 25 cm apart, all facing the outer side of the bed so the runners grow out evenly on one side.

parts.title: Let them run in the warm months
parts.how: The mothers send out runners in the warm, long days from about May to August. Keep the bed weeded and watered while the runners grow.

parts.title: Root the daughter plants
parts.how: As each young daughter plant forms on a runner, press it onto the soil of the bed or into a small bag of soil set beside it, while it is still joined to the mother. Cut the runner stem only after the daughter has made its own roots.

parts.title: Pull out off types and sick plants
parts.how: Walk the bed often and pull out any plant that does not look like the variety, and any sick plant, so their runners do not end up in the new field.

ways.note: Runners set out in October to November usually start giving berries around December, and picking goes on every few days until about April or May.

mistakes: Trying to grow strawberry in the hot lowlands, where it flowers poorly and the plants decline.
Using runners from old or sickly mother plants, which carry disease into the new field.
Burying the crown when planting, which rots the plant.
Planting during the typhoon months, when rain and flooding destroy plants and runners.
Leaving runners to grow while the plants bear, which gives fewer and smaller berries.
better: Buy clean, disease free planting stock and renew mother plants every year.
Have the soil tested. Strawberry likes loamy soil near pH 5.5 to 6.5.
Grow under a simple rain shelter or on raised elevated beds to stretch the season and save berries from rain.
Use drip irrigation under plastic mulch to save scarce water.
Scout weekly for mites and aphids and use integrated pest management, with predatory mites where available.
Rotate strawberry beds with other crops to cut soil diseases.
